newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN says 1,100 killed by Burundi army in Oct-Nov.
newsitem.headline: UN says 1,100 killed by Burundi army in Oct-Nov.

text.p: The United Nations said on Wednesday that Burundi's army killed at least 1,100 people in October and November, including hundreds of Hutu refugees returning from east Zaire.

The U.N. human rights office, in reports based on its investigations and eye-witness testimony, said Hutu rebels battling the Tutsi-dominated army also killed scores of civilians in the same period in the tiny central African country.

It warned that an already alarming situation had been made worse by the mass influx of Burundian Hutu refugees fleeing an ethnic Tutsi rebellion in eastern Zaire. The U.N. refugee agency says more than 50,000 Burundian Hutus have come home so far.

"The human rights situation in November could be described as alarming with a series of massacres, arbitrary arrests, pillage and destruction of property perpetrated by the two sides to the conflict," the reports said.
Human rights observers reported that confrontations between troops and the rebels were becoming more explosive, with Hutu guerrillas using mortars and the army striking with planes.
Rebel attacks were triggering reprisal killings almost every day by the army, and civilians were being caught in the middle.
The reports said that both rebel and government troops were responsible for the killings, but put most of the blame squarely on the army.
The U.N. human rights office said the influx of Hutu refugees had led to a big increase in arbitrary arrests and disappearances.
It said it was not in a position to verify every single one of the massacres because travel in the country had become increasingly difficult due to the spreading conflict.

In the biggest of the many listed massacres, the U.N. said between 200 and 400 Burundian Hutu returnees from east Zaire were killed and some 200 others wounded by the army with bullets and grenades in a church in Murambi village in the troubled northwestern Cibitoke region on October 21.

It said returnees were grouped inside and outside the church by the army and told to stay calm and get some sleep at dusk. Soon afterwards, the army attacked the church with grenades and firearms, the report said.
Human rights observers who later visited the area reported 258 bodies dumped in two mass graves. Eyewitnesses put the death toll higher at 435, the report said.
It quoted eyewitnesses as saying: "The soldiers came back the next day to take the bullets and grenades they'd forgotton at the site."

Other major ncidents included 123 people killed in central Bururi region on October 31, some 100 in central Gitega between November 2 and 4 following a rebel attack and another 40 in the same area between November 17 and 19.

At least 150,000 people have been killed in Burundi in a three-year war between Hutu rebels and the army. Human rights observers and diplomats say the number of army killings have soared since it grabbed power in a military coup in June.
Minority Tutsis in Burundi are outnumbered four-to-one by Hutus. Extremist Tutsis say that for every Tutsi killed, 10 Hutus must be killed in revenge.
The army denies it is killing Hutus.
